questions.q: How did the politics of 'Mandal' and 'Mandir' reshape Indian politics after 1989?
answer: From 1989, Indian politics was transformed by two powerful developments, often called Mandal and Mandir, along with the rise of coalition governments.

answer.text: In 1990 the government of V.P. Singh implemented the Mandal Commission's recommendation to reserve government jobs for the Other Backward Classes. This brought caste to the centre of politics, sparked protests, and led to the greater political assertion of backward and Dalit communities, and the rise of parties representing them.

At the same time, the Ram Janmabhoomi movement over the disputed site at Ayodhya intensified, culminating in the demolition of the Babri Masjid in 1992. This sharpened religious divisions and contributed to the rise of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

Together with the economic reforms of 1991 and the growth of regional parties, these developments ended one-party dominance and ushered in an era of coalition governments and competitive multi-party politics.

answer: Thus Mandal and Mandir reshaped Indian politics around caste, religion and coalitions.

questions.q: How did the rise of coalition politics change governance in India after 1989?

answer.text: Indian politics entered an era of coalitions, as no single party could win a majority on its own at the centre.

list: Several parties had to come together to form the government
Regional parties became crucial partners in national coalitions

answer.text: Power became more shared and negotiated.

list: Governments had to accommodate the views and interests of many partners, giving regions a bigger voice
It made government more representative but sometimes less stable, requiring constant consensus-building
